name: Keybridge
one_liner: Finds the static cloud keys your workloads use across AWS, GCP, Azure, CI and on-prem, then replaces them with free native federation, priced per account, not per workload.

buyer.role: Head of platform / DevOps lead (at smaller firms the VP Engineering or the first security hire)
buyer.company_profile: Software companies with 50-1,000 employees running workloads on two or more of AWS, GCP and Azure plus CI (GitHub Actions, GitLab) and some on-prem or edge hosts; 200-5,000 workloads, so per-workload pricing ($20/workload/month) becomes a five- or six-figure annual bill; still carrying long-lived IAM user keys and service-account JSON keys between environments, often flagged by an auditor, a leaked-key incident or a SOC 2 finding.

user: Platform and DevOps engineers who wire workloads (Kubernetes pods, Lambdas, CI jobs, VMs, third-party tools) to cloud APIs and today rotate or paste static keys when a tool does not support the provider's native credential chain.

problem.summary: Every cloud now offers free short-lived workload credentials, but each mechanism (IRSA, EKS Pod Identity, IAM Roles Anywhere, GCP and Azure workload identity federation) works only inside its own tooling and needs per-pair trust setup. Tools lag the mechanisms, so teams fall back to static keys whenever a workload crosses a cloud, a CI system or an on-prem boundary. Paid fixes charge per workload or identity, which punishes workload-heavy mid-market teams.

evidence.claim: Vault's AWS secrets engine lacked support for IAM Roles Anywhere, leaving workloads outside AWS without short-lived role credentials through the tool teams already pay for.
External Secrets did not work with the new EKS Pod Identity Agent, which injects credentials through a different endpoint than IRSA.
Vault's client did not follow the AWS SDK default credential chain in IAM auth mode, so profile- and role-based setups failed.
Bun's S3 client could only be authorised with an explicit access key and secret, not the role credentials of the Lambda or Fargate runtime.
Users want the AWS SDK to pick up a role ARN with the environment credential provider for environments where web identity is not available.
ECR's 12-hour credential expiry forces teams on a third-party GPU platform to refresh credentials manually, and they ask for permanent keys instead.
Per-identity and per-client pricing scales with machine count (Infisical Pro $20-23/identity, Aembit $20/workload), penalising workload-heavy teams.

why_now.summary: The free federation building blocks are now complete across the big three: AWS added IAM outbound identity federation (STS GetWebIdentityToken, at no additional cost, in all commercial, GovCloud and China Regions), so AWS workloads can present short-lived JWTs to GCP, Azure and SaaS; Google Cloud and Microsoft Entra already accept such tokens via workload identity federation. What is missing is the cross-cloud wiring, inventory and fallbacks for tools that do not support them. Meanwhile leaked static secrets keep growing: GitGuardian counted 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025 (+34% year over year), found that over 64% of valid secrets from 2022 were still valid in January 2026, and that 59% of machines compromised by Shai-Hulud 2 were CI/CD runners.

features.feature: Read-only static-key inventory: connects to AWS, GCP and Azure accounts and GitHub/GitLab orgs, lists long-lived IAM user access keys, GCP service-account keys and Entra app secrets, and shows where each one is used (last-used source IP/service, CI secret names) and which cloud boundary it crosses.
features.why: Gives the buyer a number to act on and a reason to pay before anything is changed; uses read-only APIs so security review is light.

features.feature: Federation plan generator: for each key, proposes the native free replacement (IRSA / EKS Pod Identity, IAM Roles Anywhere, AWS outbound federation to GCP/Azure, GCP and Entra workload identity federation, GitHub/GitLab OIDC) and emits a Terraform/OpenTofu pull request with the trust policies and least-privilege role.
features.why: The credential issuance is free and native; the work buyers lack is the per-pair trust configuration, which is where they give up and keep static keys.

features.feature: Open-source credential helper (credential_process / exec plugin / sidecar) that turns a native identity into credentials for the target cloud via the default credential chain, for tools that do not support Pod Identity, Roles Anywhere or cross-cloud federation.
features.why: Covers the tool-lag cases in the evidence (Vault, External Secrets, Bun, ECR refresh) without asking upstream tools to change; also the open-source adoption channel.

features.feature: Cutover tracking and drift alerts: marks each static key as replaced, verifies the federated path is in use, then prompts deactivation; alerts when a new long-lived key appears.
features.why: Turns a one-off migration into a recurring control that auditors (SOC 2, ISO 27001) can see, which justifies a subscription.

features.feature: Evidence export: per-account report of keys found, replaced and remaining, with dates.
features.why: Gives the platform lead something to hand the auditor or CISO; this report is what the buyer is paying for.

out_of_scope: Issuing our own credentials, running a token broker in the request path or a proxy that injects credentials (Aembit's model); v1 only configures the clouds' free native mechanisms.
General secrets storage and rotation of database or SaaS API keys (Vault, Infisical, Akeyless).
AI agent / MCP identity and human access (PAM, SSO).
Policy engines with conditional access; NHI posture scoring across SaaS (Cyera Identity / Oasis).

competitors.name: Native cloud federation (AWS IRSA / EKS Pod Identity / IAM Roles Anywhere / outbound identity federation, GCP and Entra workload identity federation)
competitors.how_we_differ: Free and what we build on, not against: we discover where it is not used yet, generate the cross-cloud trust configuration and fill gaps for tools that do not support it. Each cloud documents only its own side.

competitors.name: Aembit Workload IAM
competitors.how_we_differ: Aembit runs a policy-based workload IAM platform at $20/workload/month (Teams) with a free tier of 10 workloads. We charge a flat price per cloud account with unlimited workloads, and leave no broker in the request path, so nothing breaks if we disappear.

competitors.name: Infisical
competitors.how_we_differ: Infisical is a secrets manager priced per identity ($20/identity/month annually, Pro); its AWS auth still issues its own tokens. We remove secrets instead of storing them, and do not charge per identity.

competitors.name: HCP Vault Dedicated (HashiCorp/IBM)
competitors.how_we_differ: Vault generates dynamic AWS credentials but per-client pricing and cluster operation make it a heavy buy for this goal, and it lagged new AWS mechanisms (Roles Anywhere). We are a lightweight layer over native federation.

competitors.name: Teleport Machine & Workload Identity
competitors.how_we_differ: Bundled into Teleport Enterprise and billed per protected resource, quote-only. We are self-serve with a public price and need no Teleport deployment.

competitors.name: Cyera Identity (formerly Oasis NHI Security Cloud)
competitors.how_we_differ: Enterprise NHI discovery and posture, $100,000/12-month starter pack on AWS Marketplace. We do a narrower job (cloud static keys to federation) and remediate it, for mid-market budgets.

competitors.name: SPIFFE / SPIRE (open source)
competitors.how_we_differ: Free workload attestation and identity, but a system to deploy and operate, mostly certificate-based and Kubernetes-centric. We reuse the identities clouds already issue and need no new infrastructure.

differentiation: The clouds now give short-lived workload credentials away; what mid-market teams lack is the time to find every static key and wire up each cross-cloud trust. Keybridge does that job, opens Terraform pull requests to native mechanisms and adds an open-source helper for tools that lag. Flat per-account pricing means 2,000 workloads cost the same as 20, and no proxy or broker sits in the request path, so there is no lock-in and no new outage risk.

build.team: 2 engineers (cloud IAM and Terraform depth) + 1 founder-seller
hardest_parts: Attributing where a static key is used (CloudTrail last-used data, CI secret references, GCP/Azure logs) accurately enough that a generated replacement does not break production.

Generating correct least-privilege trust policies for every source-target pair (EKS, ECS, Lambda, GKE, AKS, VMs, GitHub/GitLab, on-prem with Roles Anywhere certificates) and keeping up as the clouds change these APIs.
Getting read-only access to several cloud accounts approved at mid-market companies without a long security review.
Keeping the credential helper compatible with SDK default chains across languages and runtimes (Go, Python, Node, Bun, JVM).

pricing.model: Subscription per connected cloud account / project / subscription, unlimited workloads; free tier for discovery; open-source credential helper.
pricing.entry_price: Free inventory for up to 3 cloud accounts; Team $400/month (billed annually) for up to 10 cloud accounts plus GitHub/GitLab orgs, unlimited workloads, remediation PRs and drift alerts; $30/month per additional account.
pricing.rationale: A team with 500 workloads would pay about $10,000/month on Aembit Teams or Infisical Pro list prices; $400/month undercuts that by an order of magnitude while still a meaningful recurring line for a 3-person company. Pricing on accounts, not workloads, removes the per-machine penalty that the input names as the main paid-market gap, and matches how buyers think about cloud estate. Enterprise NHI platforms (Cyera Identity at $100k/year) set the ceiling.

comparables.price: Free up to 10 workloads; Teams from $20/workload/month

go_to_market.first_customers: Ten 50-500 person SaaS or data companies running on AWS plus GCP or Azure (often for BigQuery, Vertex/Azure OpenAI or a customer-mandated cloud), with GitHub Actions CI and a few hundred to a few thousand workloads; each has at least one SOC 2 finding or near-miss about long-lived cloud keys, a platform team of 2-6 and no Vault or Teleport deployment.
go_to_market.channel: Open-source credential helper and a free 'static key report' that runs read-only in minutes; content and Terraform modules for each cross-cloud pair (e.g. 'EKS to BigQuery without a JSON key'); answers in the GitHub issues where users hit tool lag; listing in the AWS and GCP marketplaces to draw on committed spend; later, SOC 2 auditors and compliance platforms as referral partners.
go_to_market.wedge: The free key report: it shows a platform lead how many long-lived keys cross cloud boundaries today, then converts on the first automated pull request that removes one.

risks: Bundling (high): AWS, Google and Microsoft keep adding free federation and could add cross-cloud setup wizards or key-usage reports; IAM Access Analyzer and cloud security posture tools (Wiz, native CSPMs) already flag old access keys. The product must stay a remediation tool, not a finding list.

Crowding and consolidation: Aembit, Infisical, Akeyless, Teleport and Cyera Identity all sell workload identity; Aembit's free 10-workload tier and $20/workload Teams plan compete directly for small estates, and acquirers (Palo Alto/CyberArk, Cyera) can bundle discovery into larger deals.

Low price ceiling: the core value is configuration of free mechanisms, so buyers may treat it as a one-off migration and churn once their keys are gone; drift alerts and audit evidence must justify ongoing payment.

Technical: a wrong generated trust policy or misattributed key usage can break production or over-grant access, and read-only access to many accounts is itself a sensitive permission buyers must trust.
Thin and unstable demand signal: the theme scored only 0.41 on stability and the evidence is mostly AWS-only tool-lag issues, so the cross-cloud need is inferred rather than shown directly.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: Mid-market platform teams will pay a recurring subscription to get rid of cross-cloud static keys, rather than doing the native federation setup themselves or taking Aembit's free tier.
riskiest_assumption.test: Run a landing page plus a manual 'static key report' offer (customer runs a published read-only script; we return a per-key replacement plan) to 40 platform leads from DevOps communities and the GitHub issues in the evidence; ask those who receive a report to pre-commit to the $400/month plan with a signed letter of intent or annual prepayment at a discount.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: At least 10 of 40 run the script, the median report finds 15 or more long-lived keys used across a cloud or CI boundary, and at least 3 sign an LOI or prepay within two weeks.

open_questions: How many long-lived cloud keys does a typical 50-500 person multi-cloud company actually have crossing boundaries, and how many workloads depend on them?
Is the cross-cloud case common enough, or is the real volume in AWS-only tool lag that AWS will fix itself?
Will buyers grant read-only access to every cloud account and CI org to a young vendor, or must the scanner run fully in their environment?
Does per-account pricing hold, or do buyers expect a one-off migration fee plus a small monitoring subscription?
Can the HCP Vault per-client price (flagged as unverified) be confirmed from a primary source to strengthen the price comparison?
How fast will AWS, Google and Microsoft ship their own cross-cloud setup tooling?
